gen-fredoka-gf-new-tegomin: Friendly and rounded, Fredoka draws every line with a single pen width, while New Tegomin brings a dignified serif with a ring-wide c. They feel like a smile beside a handshake.
gen-fredoka-gf-podkova: Fredoka leads with a pen line that never changes width, and its e opens with a clear gap. Podkova follows in a bookish text serif, and its broad c gives the soft top a traditional footing.
gen-fredoka-gf-rhodium-libre: Rhodium Libre is an editorial text serif whose brush ends lift away before each curve closes. Fredoka, up top, feels like pipe cleaner bent into letters, so the page moves from friendly to traditional.
gen-fredoka-gf-rokkitt: Single thick thread is the feeling Fredoka gives, every letter traced with an open e and a clear gap. Rokkitt's serif body has a c as open as a bent paperclip.
gen-fredoka-gf-sanchez: Approachable up top, Fredoka keeps a constant stroke from the top of each letter to the baseline. And Sanchez, a bookish text serif with a c opened like calipers, earns the dignified side of the pairing.
gen-fredoka-gf-solway: Friendly and soft, Fredoka traces its letters with one pen width and an open e, while Solway answers in a bookish serif with a flat, stencil-like weight. Fredoka is best at greeting; Solway is best at speaking with authority.
gen-fredoka-gf-yuji-boku: One unvarying pen line defines Fredoka, which makes its heading letters feel traced from a single thick thread. Yuji Boku, a dignified text serif, holds each stroke like a drawn cable and opens its c like a pulled-apart bracelet.
gen-fs-kalam-bitter: Cozy and hand-drawn, Kalam bundles its lines tightly and feels inviting from the first word, while Bitter sets a slab-serif below it. Bitter's big lowercase eye and see-through s make a long read feel dependable.
gen-fs-kalam-inter: Inviting and handwritten, Kalam sets the tone first. Its heading is at its best being casual and tightly bundled, while Inter, a plain sans, is best at big, open counters and smooth, tube-like lines.
gen-fs-kalam-mulish: Tightly bundled lines with a hand-drawn feel make Kalam the most distinctive voice here. And Mulish, a plain sans with no thick-and-thin modulation and horseshoe-open apertures, would carry a longer passage in a modern, approachable way.
